_note: WhatsDaf's own English renderings of the Hebrew commentaries on Sefaria (Vilna edition). Keys are <commentary>:<amud><segment>.<comment>. Square brackets are our clarifications. Very long Tosafot are condensed and marked "In brief".
rashi:a1.1: This is the reading: the dulfanin reproduce from people [Rashi reads “from people,” where the printed Gemara and the English have “like people”]: that if a man has relations with them, they conceive from him.
rashi:a1.2: Sons of the sea: there are fish in the sea that are half in the form of a person and half in the form of a fish. (Rashi adds an Old French gloss.)
rashi:a2.1: Any species whose male’s testicles are external, such as wild and domestic animals, gives birth to an actual fetus.
rashi:a2.2: And any species whose male’s testicles are internal: the female lays eggs.
rashi:a3.1: A goose: a domestic goose and a wild goose are diverse kinds with regard to mating them, since the males are not alike: this one’s testicles are external and that one’s are internal.
rashi:a4.1: Its male organ: the member. And the wild goose’s male organ is internal.
rashi:a7.1: And the following day he rose early: before daybreak, and found an egg in it, it is permitted, since it was not laid on the night of the Festival but the day before, as a chicken does not lay at night, as was taught above. If most of it emerged, it is permitted, since we go by the emergence of the majority.
rashi:a9.1: Any whose intercourse and gestation are identical: such as a sheep and a goat, both of which mate face to the back of the neck, and whose days of gestation are identical, as they carry five months; they give birth if one mates with the other’s species.
rashi:a10.1: The Divine Presence [spoke] with them: as it is stated: “And the Lord spoke to the fish” (Jonah 2:11).
rashi:a12.1: After twenty-one days: after it has conceived from the rooster, its egg takes twenty-one days to be completed.
rashi:a12.2: Luz: (Rashi adds an Old French gloss) [a tree] on which small nuts grow; from the time it flowers until its fruit is ripe is twenty-two days [so the printed Rashi; the baraita says twenty-one]. [Rashi takes luz as a small-nut tree; the English “almond” follows the view Tosafot cite from Riva.]
rashi:a12.3: A dog after fifty days: [by then] the form of the fetus is completed.
rashi:a12.4: And corresponding to them among trees is grain: according to the one who says (Berakhot 40a) that the tree from which Adam ate was wheat, grain is called a tree.
rashi:a13.1: Date palm: on which dates grow.
rashi:a13.3: Monkey: (Rashi adds an Old French gloss.)
rashi:a13.4: Kipof [the long-tailed ape]: it is like a monkey and has a tail. (Rashi adds a German gloss.)
rashi:a14.1: A viper: it conceives seventy years after it was born.
rashi:a14.2: And the days of its gestation: from the time of the flowering until the time the fruit is completed.
rashi:a14.3: Mukhsasim: a kind of benot shuaḥ [a variety of fig], but not benot shuaḥ proper.
rashi:a15.1: From where are these matters derived: that the snake’s gestation is seven years.
rashi:a15.2: If it was cursed more than the domesticated animals, is it not all the more so more than the wild animals: for [domesticated animals] are lower than wild animals, since a goat takes five months and a cat fifty-two [days]. And one cannot say that “from all the beasts” means the lion or the viper, for if so, let it write “from all the beasts” and it would not need “animals.”
rashi:a16.1: Rather, it wrote both of them to tell you, etc.: and this is the meaning: it is cursed from all the domesticated animals as much as [the domesticated animal] is cursed more than the wild animal. Just as the domesticated animal was cursed more than the wild animal one to seven, and what is that? A donkey compared to a cat, for a year holds seven times fifty-two [days], so it was cursed more than the domesticated animal, namely large non-kosher livestock, one to seven: large non-kosher livestock carries twelve months, and seven times twelve months, which is one to seven, makes seven years.
tosafot:a1.1: The dulfanin reproduce from people: this is the reading of the Kuntres [Rashi], and so it is evident in the Tosefta (chapter 1): “they bear and raise young from people.”
tosafot:a8.1: Say most of it emerged and returned: from here they permit buying eggs on the night of the second Festival day of the Diaspora, except for the two Festival days of Rosh HaShana, since they are one sanctity.
tosafot:a12.1: A chicken, twenty-one days, and corresponding to it among trees, the luz: the Kuntres [Rashi] explains (Old French gloss), on which small nuts grow. Riva explains almonds, called (Old French gloss), since for “nuts and almonds” (Genesis 43:11) the Targum Yerushalmi renders luzim, and “a rod of an almond tree” (Jeremiah 1:11) is rendered “a rod of luz.” And some explain “a rod of an almond tree” as one in twenty-one, like the days from the seventeenth of Tammuz to the Ninth of Av [twenty-one days]. “And the almond tree shall blossom” (Ecclesiastes 12:5) is rendered shigda, and “it bore ripe almonds” (Numbers 17:23) is rendered “it ripened shigdin.” We also say: “And the almond tree shall blossom”: this is the luz of the spine, from which the dead are destined to be revived in the future; and luz is the Aramaic for shaked [almond] (Vayikra Rabba).
tosafot:a12.2: Among trees, the mulberry: there is no proof from here that one recites over them “Who creates the fruit of the tree,” for we likewise say “among trees, grain,” which follows the one who says (Berakhot 40a) that the tree from which Adam ate was wheat. Evidently grain is called a tree, and yet one does not recite “fruit of the tree” over it. However, over mulberries that grow on a tree one does recite “fruit of the tree,” but not over field mulberries [that grow on a low plant], for if you take the fruit the stem does not grow back and produce again, and one recites “fruit of the tree” only where the stem grows back and produces.
tosafot:a13.1: Bardelas: Rashi explains afa; in the first chapter of Sanhedrin (15b) Rashi explains (Old French gloss); and at the end of the first chapter of Bava Kamma (16a) we say that the bardelas is the afa, and we say that the tzavua [hyena] is the afa, and “the valley of Tzevo’im” (I Samuel 13:18) is rendered “the plain of Afaya.” But the bardelas here seems to be like the (Old French gloss), and it gives birth after three years, since [the baraita] lists the viper [efe] separately, at seventy years. There are two kinds of bardelas.
tosafot:a13.2: The kof and the kipof: [the kipof] is a kind of wild animal, since they are counted together with the elephant. In chapter HaRo’eh (Berakhot 57b) it says that all kinds of animals are good in a dream except for the elephant and the kipof. In chapter HaMappelet (Nidda 23a) we say: “Some say Rabbi Meir says: since their eyes are set in front like those of a person.” And “the kos and the yanshuf” (Leviticus 11:17) are rendered kaya and kafofa. There is also another kipof, a kind of bird: in chapter Elu Tereifot (Ḥullin 63a) it says the tinshemet is the ba’ot among birds, and it says the ba’ot among birds is the kipof. Some read kipod, with a dalet, following “the ka’at and the kipod shall possess it” (Isaiah 34:11). But if one reads kipof, and there are two kinds of kipof among birds, then when it explains that the ba’ot among birds is the kipof, how would we know whether it speaks of the yanshuf or of the tinshemet?
tosafot:a13.3: In brief: Benot shuaḥ: on the mishna in Shevi’it (5:1) that their Sabbatical year falls in the second year, the Yerushalmi explains that they set fruit every year, and fruit set in one year is not finished until three years. This is not like Rabbeinu Ḥananel, who explained, on the thirty trees of which only twenty yield each year, that benot shuaḥ yield every three years. In Avoda Zara (14a) the reading is “mukhsasim, benot shuaḥ” as one kind, and that is its name. A difficulty: the mishna in Demai (1:1) lists them among the lenient items that the unlearned were not suspected of, implying they are not a valued fruit; Avoda Zara (14a) explains them as white figs; and Nedarim (27a) treats benot sheva and white figs as two kinds (“had I known benot sheva were in the basket…”). Tosafot conclude that benot shuaḥ and benot sheva are both kinds of fig: benot shuaḥ are the poor ones, as the Demai and Shevi’it mishnayot imply, and benot sheva the good ones, as Shevi’it (5) and Nedarim (27a) imply. Presumably Adam ate of the good ones; they are called sheva after the seven days of mourning, and shuaḥ because they caused him to be bowed down, and the damage is ascribed to the poor kind. Open on Sefaria for the full text.
tosafot:a16.1: And what is that? A donkey compared to a cat: since a cat is fifty-two days. And it is puzzling, according to the one who says that a dog is a kind of wild animal, as in tractate Beitza (25b), “three are bold: the dog among wild animals”: let it take a donkey compared to a dog, which is more defective, since the dog is fifty days. One can say: this number is more exact, since it comes to a year.
gershom:a1.1: Rav Yehuda said: Sons of the sea: a person of the sea. Any whose testicles are outside, outside its belly, such as a domestic animal whose testicles are outside its body: its female gives birth.
gershom:a2.1: Any whose male’s testicles are inside, such as birds: its female lays eggs.
gershom:a3.1: Diverse kinds with each other: with regard to driving them together.
gershom:a4.1: Rather, whose male organ is outside, its member: [its female] gives birth.
gershom:a5.1: Whose male organ is inside lays eggs. And the wild goose too, although its testicles are outside, its male organ, its member, is inside, and that is why it lays eggs.
gershom:a6.1: It is permitted to eat it on the Festival: since it was not laid on the Festival, nor at night, as it does not lay at night; certainly it is from yesterday.
gershom:a7.1: But didn’t he examine on the Festival eve? Say most of it emerged from the chicken’s belly on the Festival eve and returned; that is why he did not find it when he examined. And since most of it emerged and returned, that egg which returned is laid even at night, and it is permitted to eat it on the Festival. But in the first place a chicken does not lay an egg at night, as we said; therefore it is permitted.
gershom:a8.1: Any whose intercourse and gestation are identical: such as any small kosher livestock, which give birth after five months; that is, their gestation is identical, and their intercourse is identical, face opposite the back of the neck. They give birth to and raise one another: e.g., a ewe from a he-goat and a goat from a ram give birth from one another. And “raise”: their offspring survive. And likewise any large livestock whose gestation and intercourse are identical.
gershom:a9.1: A chicken gives birth after twenty-one days, after its cluster of eggs is completed; and corresponding to it among trees is the luz, from the time it buds until its fruit is finished, twenty-one days. And some say: for twenty-one days it sits on its eggs. [The note ends with an unclear abbreviation.]
gershom:a10.1: A dog, fifty days [the printed text reads fifty-two, corrected to fifty]: from the time it conceives until it gives birth.
gershom:a11.1: And corresponding to it among trees is the fig: from the time of budding until the fruit is finished.
gershom:a12.1: And corresponding to them among trees is grain: for grain is called a tree, according to the one who says the tree from which Adam ate was wheat. Six months from the time of sowing until they form ears.
gershom:a13.1: Shuaḥ [benot shuaḥ, rendered “white fig” in the English]: white figs. And the gestation of the carob is its budding, the last three years of the seventy years.
gershom:a15.1: If it was cursed more than the domesticated animals: for small domesticated animals are later to give birth than small, little wild animals, is it not all the more so? For small domesticated animals give birth at five months, and a small wild animal at fifty-two days, such as a cat and a dog.
gershom:a16.1: Rather, why was “from all the beasts” stated? To tell you: just as the domesticated animals were cursed more than the wild animals one to seven, and what is that? A donkey compared to a cat, for a cat is fifty-two days and large non-kosher livestock twelve months, which is 365 days; 350 days is seven times fifty, and the fifteen that remain make it seven times fifty-two for the cat. So too it was cursed more than the non-kosher animal, one to seven, which comes to seven years.
gershom:a17.1: And say: just as the wild animals were cursed more than the domesticated animals one to three, and what is that? A lion compared to a donkey, etc.
rashi:b1.1: Is it written “from all the beasts and from all the animals,” that we should expound: from all the beasts, which were cursed more than the domesticated animals?
rashi:b1.2: [“From all the animals” is written: implying that it was cursed as much as the most cursed of the domesticated animals; and among large livestock you have none more cursed than the donkey.]
rashi:b2.1: So too it was cursed more than the domesticated animals one to three: such as small kosher livestock, whose gestation is five months, and three times that is fifteen.
rashi:b3.1: If you wish, say “from all the animals”: which implies, from all the animals, the most cursed one.
rashi:b3.2: And if you wish, say: it was stated as a curse; therefore impose upon it the severest curse you can expound from the verse. One could similarly challenge: say, just as the domesticated animals were cursed more than the wild animals one to two, and what is that? A donkey compared to a fox, so it was cursed more than the donkey one to two, which comes to two years. But one can answer: impose the curse upon it. Moreover, “from all the animals and from all the beasts” is written, which implies [it is measured] by the domesticated animal whose curse exceeds that of the wild animal, and we found the donkey cursed more than the cat, one to seven.
rashi:b4.1: After how long does it conceive and give birth: how long its gestation stays in its belly.
rashi:b4.3: But they engaged in intercourse: and had they been pregnant they would not have engaged in intercourse, for the way of a wild or domesticated animal is that once it has conceived it does not accept a male.
rashi:b5.1: But they are wise: those elders, and they get to the bottom of a matter.
rashi:b6.2: When he arrived there: at their city.
rashi:b6.3: Doing an animal: cutting up an animal.
rashi:b7.1: And did I say to you the head of the animal? Said as a question [I did not].
rashi:b7.2: Sagi: step forward and go before me.
rashi:b7.3: Carry a bundle of reeds: take a bundle of reeds, and when you get there, opposite the entrance, stand the bundle up on the ground.
rashi:b7.4: Like one who is resting: like a person who stops to rest.
rashi:b8.3: Outside: so that none of the elders would go out.
rashi:b8.4: Inside: so that they would not let anyone enter. And when those elders saw an entering footprint they killed [the outer guards]. For the threshold of the room was thick, and they would pour bran or dust on it, and a person’s steps showed in it. When they saw an entering footprint they killed the [outer] guards, for letting him come in; and when they saw an exiting footprint they killed the [inner] ones, for letting him go out. And the guards would not kill anyone, unless one forced his way entirely inside or one went entirely outside.
rashi:b9.1: He reversed: Rabbi Yehoshua reversed his sandal and stood on the threshold, and there appeared one step entering and one step exiting. The guards pushed him and he went out. When the elders came and saw this, they imagined that there were two people, one entering and one leaving, and they killed all the guards. Afterward Rabbi Yehoshua went in.
rashi:b10.1: Youngsters above: in the upper story. They intended harm: one who greets the upper ones first, the lower ones kill him, saying, “We are the elders, and you should have greeted us first”; and one who greets the elders, the young men kill him, saying, “Are we not more important than they, for we are above and they are below?”
rashi:b11.1: What is your business: what do you want here?
rashi:b11.2: If so: that you are wise, let us ask you.
rashi:b11.3: If you defeat me: if you overcome me.
rashi:b12.1: Greater than it: of better lineage than the first, and he asks for her. Surely he should learn: since they did not give him the first, all the more so this one.
rashi:b12.2: Sikhta: a peg. (Rashi adds an Old French gloss.)
rashi:b12.3: He stuck it low: he lowered his hand and stuck it into the wall at a place where there was no hole, and it did not go in; [he stuck it] high: he raised [his hand] and stuck it where there was a hole, and it went in.
rashi:b13.1: A man who lends and repossesses: who lent money to his fellow and was repaid only with difficulty, in that he seized property from buyers.
rashi:b13.2: Why would he see fit to lend again: to others, and not take a lesson from the first?
rashi:b13.3: To the agma: to the forest.
rashi:b13.4: He cut a first bundle: he cut a first bundle and could not lift it onto his shoulder.
rashi:b13.5: He cuts more and places it upon it: since he needs the help of others anyway, until someone happens by and lifts it for him. So too this one: since he lost on his first trust, he goes on trusting others until he is matched with a trustworthy person and profits by him.
rashi:b14.1: Matters of kedi: words of wind. Another version: matters of kazav, words of falsehood.
rashi:b14.3: And a note was hanging: a document on the newborn’s neck.
rashi:b14.4: These are matters of kedi: these are words of wind.
rashi:b17.1: Of bran: make me ropes of bran; and if you do not do what I ask, I too will not do what you ask.
rashi:b17.3: Pull out threads from it for me: draw threads out of it for me, the way women draw threads out of a garment and sew it with them.
rashi:b17.4: Gardi: (Rashi adds an Old French gloss.)
rashi:b18.1: A field of knives, with what does one cut it: a bed of knives, with what does one harvest it?
rashi:b20.1: And a chick that died: a chick that died in its shell.
rashi:b20.2: Show us a utensil that is not worth its damage: show us a utensil that is not worth the loss it causes.
rashi:b20.4: It did not enter the gate: for it was longer and wider than the entrance.
rashi:b20.5: Bring axes: (Rashi adds an Old French gloss.)
rashi:b20.6: And break it: the entrance of the building and the wall, until it goes in.
rashi:b21.1: He brought them: to go onto the ship, since he had defeated them. He brought them one by one, each by himself, and put each into a room.
rashi:b21.2: And when he saw sixty bistarkei: he thought, all my colleagues will come here.
rashi:b21.3: He said to him: Rabbi Yehoshua.
rashi:b21.4: To the sailor: the ship’s captain.
rashi:b21.5: Release your ship: untie your ship and go.
tosafot:b2.1: One to three; and what is that? A goat compared to a cat: here it would have been better to take a goat compared to a dog, according to the one who says (Kilayim 8:6) [that the dog] is a kind of wild animal, since their numbers fit one to three more exactly. But it preferred to challenge according to everyone.
gershom:b1.1: And say: just as the domesticated animals were cursed more than the wild animals one to three, and what is that? A goat compared to a cat: for a cat is fifty-two days and a goat five months, which is three times fifty-two.
gershom:b2.1: If you wish, say: “from all the animals” is written: from the domesticated animal that is cursed more than the wild animal, that is, one to seven, as we said.
gershom:b3.1: If you wish, say: it is a curse; since it is being cursed, we place it after the domesticated animal that was cursed most relative to the wild animal.
gershom:b4.1: Impose upon it: more of a curse.
gershom:b5.1: They mated them: a male snake on the female, and they placed them under guard, and it gave birth after three years.
gershom:b6.1: Those: that gave birth after three years were certainly pregnant at the outset, four years before they mated them.
gershom:b7.1: But they engaged in intercourse: when they mated them; and had the female been pregnant, it certainly would not have accepted a male, for such is the way of all animals: after they conceive they do not accept a male.
gershom:b8.1: They too: the snakes engage in intercourse like a person, face to face; and since they engage like a person, they also engage after they have conceived, like a person.
gershom:b9.1: But they are wise: the elders of the school of Atuna, in other matters, and they are wise in this too, in saying three years.
gershom:b10.1: We are wiser than they: we know every matter better than they do.
gershom:b11.1: Go defeat them: that is, engage them in matters of wisdom and make a condition with them that if you defeat them they will go with you; and bring them to me.
gershom:b12.1: He said to him: How many are those elders? He said to him: Sixty.
gershom:b14.1: When he arrived there: at their place, at a butcher shop, etc.
gershom:b15.1: Stand it up: opposite their entrance, like one who is resting; it will look to people as though you are doing this to rest from your load, and they will not notice you, and that way I will know their entrance.
gershom:b16.1: He found bran inside: bran was scattered there, inside the entrance and outside. And some say darbonei are guards, outside and inside.
gershom:b17.1: For if they saw: the mark of an entering foot, they would kill the outer guards, who let a man in; and if they saw the mark of an exiting foot, they would kill the inner guards.
gershom:b18.1: Rabbi Yehoshua went and watched for the time when the guards slept, and reversed one sandal, the heel in front, and left the other as it was; and one appeared to be entering and the other leaving. Once they saw the steps like this, they killed all the guards.
gershom:b19.1: He found the youngsters above and the elders below: in order to bring a charge against a person whether he greets these first or those.
gershom:b21.1: He stuck it into the wall low, in a place opposite a stone where there was no hole: it did not go in. He stuck it high, in a place between stone and stone where there was a hole, and it went in. So too, sometimes, when one asks for a woman of better lineage than the first, perhaps she will be his destined match.
gershom:b22.1: A man who lends money to someone and repossesses: when he comes to collect it, he seizes it with distress, through the court. Why would he see fit to lend again to another person? He said to them: A man goes to the marsh and cuts a first bundle of reeds, and it was so big that he cannot load it; and he goes on cutting and places more on that bundle. He adds, cuts and places it on top only because he thinks: until someone happens by who will help me lift it onto my shoulders. So too this one lends again, since he thinks: this last debtor will be easier than the first.
gershom:b23.1: Matters of nonsense: parables of falsehood.
gershom:b24.1: He uttered a Name and suspended himself between sky and earth. He said to them: Bring up bricks and mortar to me in the air; and they could not.
gershom:b25.1: He said: Pull out threads from it for me; that is, take threads out of it for me and I will sew it.
gershom:b26.1: A field of knives: a bed of knives.
gershom:b27.1: And a chick: a chick that died inside its egg.
gershom:b28.1: Show us a utensil that is not worth its damage: that is, show us a utensil that is not worth the loss it causes.
gershom:b29.1: He brought a mat and spread it out, and when spread out it could not go in through the entrance.
gershom:b30.1: He said to them: Bring axes and hatchets and break down the gateway, so that it can go out through it. He said: This is the utensil, etc.
gershom:b31.1: He answered them everything they asked him and defeated them, and brought them onto the ship, each one in his own room.
